 A 1440W AC input fills the 1152Wh pack in about an hour. The 500W solar input takes roughly 2.8 to 3.3 hours on its own, or about an hour when combined with wall power on a hybrid setup.

 Scaling from 1024Wh to 5120Wh turns a weekend station into a multi-day system without new wiring or a second battery to manage. The 1400W AC input and 800W solar input on standard MC4 connectors mean your existing panels will work.

 The 4500W surge figure is optimistic. Reviewers report the inverter commonly tripping between 2050W and 2200W, so treat the 2000W continuous rating as the real ceiling and leave a margin for compressor loads.

 Fridge Runtime as the Real Benchmark
 Fridge duty cycle is the truest test of a station because it runs 24 hours a day in summer heat. At 9W idle and a measured 32 hours on a dual-door unit, this station outlasts most 2kWh competitors for the most common RV load.

 The 4000W peak is enough for most window and RV air conditioning units, which is a step up from every 1kWh station here. The 2400W continuous rating handles a microwave and fridge compressor together without strain.

 How to Size and Choose a Portable Power Station for an RV
 Sizing mistakes come down to two numbers: how much energy your loads consume, and how much power they draw at once. Get both right and the choice becomes obvious.
 Step 1: Work Out Your Daily Load in Watt-Hours
 A 12V compressor fridge typically cycles 8 to 10 hours a day. A 1500W microwave run for six minutes a day is about 150 Wh. Add a CPAP machine at roughly 40W for eight hours, Starlink at 100W, LED lighting at 15W and a coffee maker at 800W for four minutes and a typical family of two lands near 500Wh per day. Multiply by your number of days off-grid, then add 20% for inverter losses.
 A useful sanity check comes from RV owner communities: r/RVLiving campers regularly report that a station in the 2kWh class paired with 200 to 400 watts of solar covers a whole trailer comfortably. A single 100Ah AGM house battery with 50Ah usable is the baseline these stations are usually compared against, and it is the number most buyers are trying to improve on.
 Step 2: Usable Watt-Hours Are Lower Than the Nameplate
 A 2048Wh station typically yields around 1600 to 1700Wh through the inverter, and idle draw can shave another 10 to 20W per hour. This is the single most common disappointment buyers report, and it is entirely normal. Multiply nameplate capacity by 0.8 to get a realistic daily budget.
 Step 3: Check Continuous Output and Surge
 Continuous wattage is what your appliances draw once running. Surge is the spike a compressor or pump produces on start. If a 1500W microwave shares a circuit with a compressor fridge at 150W, you need at least 1650W continuous, and 3000W of surge to be safe.
 Step 4: Weigh It Against Your Payload Rating
 This step is skipped almost everywhere else, and it is the one that keeps trailers safe. Stations range from 23.8 lb to 72 lb, and every pound counts against the payload number on your trailer’s VIN plate. If your payload is already tight, a 72 lb unit is a towing-weight problem, not a power problem. We have covered smaller options in our roundups of the best portable power stations for tailgating and the best entry-level portable power stations if the budget is the constraint.
 Step 5: Size Your Solar Input to the Station
 Match panel wattage to the solar input ceiling. A 1kWh station with 500W to 600W of input will refill in good sun, and a 200W portable panel is plenty for a weekend with a car top-up. A 2kWh station with 800W to 1200W of input pairs well with 400W of folding panels plus a 200W roof panel. Expect real-world yield well below nameplate when trees or clouds cut in, which is why r/camping boondockers in the 4kWh to 5kWh range treat solar as a supplement rather than a full replacement.
 Chemistry, Cold Weather and Storage
 LiFePO4 is the right choice for RV use in every case here, with cycle ratings from 3000 to 4000+ cycles and none of the thermal runaway concerns of NMC packs. The rule that catches people out is charging: do not charge a station that has sat below freezing, and store it between 50% and 80% charge between trips rather than empty or full.  Frequently Asked Questions
 Can a portable power station run an RV?
 Yes, for most RV appliances. A 1500W station runs a 12V compressor fridge, LED lights, a CPAP machine, a router and Starlink. A 2400W station adds a microwave and a small space heater. You cannot run a rooftop air conditioner on most units, and you cannot plug a station into a 30A pedestal to backfeed the trailer.
 How big of a portable power station do I need for an RV?
 For a weekend trip running a fridge, lights and a CPAP, 1000Wh to 1152Wh is enough. For a week of boondocking with a microwave, coffee maker and Starlink, 2000Wh to 2304Wh is the practical range. Multiply your daily watt-hour load by your trip length, add 20% for inverter losses, and match your heaviest simultaneous load to the continuous wattage rating.
 How long will a portable power station run an RV fridge?
 A 12V compressor fridge drawing about 50W runs for roughly 16 to 20 hours on a 1000Wh station and around 32 hours on a 2048Wh station with low idle consumption. Actual runtime depends on ambient temperature, fridge size, how often the door opens and the inverter overhead of the unit you choose.
 Is Jackery or EcoFlow better for an RV?
 Jackery is lighter and better suited to weekend trips: the Explorer 1000 v2 is 23.8 lb with 1070Wh and 1500W output. EF ECOFLOW delivers far more power from a similar footprint: the DELTA 3 Max reaches 3400W via X-Boost and charges from 0 to 80% in about 1.13 hours. Pick Jackery for portability, EcoFlow for high-draw appliances.
 What size solar panel do I need with an RV power station?
 Match your panels to the station’s solar input ceiling. A 1kWh station with 500W to 600W of input recharges in roughly 3 hours of full sun, and a 2kWh station with 800W to 1200W of input does the same. A 200W portable panel is a good weekend supplement; 400W plus a 200W roof panel suits multi-day trips.
 Do I need a portable power station for RV trips?
 If you camp at 30A hookups, you probably do not. If you dry camp or boondock more than a few times a year, or you run a CPAP machine, a 12V fridge or Starlink away from a site, one removes the noise, fuel and exhaust of a gas generator and lets those devices run safely indoors.
 Is it safe to run a portable power station inside the RV?
 Yes, that is the main advantage over a gas generator. Keep the unit ventilated and away from direct sun or heaters, never charge a station that has been sitting below freezing, and store it between 50% and 80% charge when it is not in use. LiFePO4 chemistry is the safer choice for enclosed spaces.
